The revolutionary terrorists were severely suppressed during World War I, with most of the leaders in jail or absconding. Consequently, in
order to create a more harmonious atmosphere for the Montague-Chelmsford reforms, the Government released most of them under a
general amnesty in early 1920. Soon after, the National Congress launched the Non-Cooperation Movement and on the urging of Gandhiji,
C.R. Das and other Leaders most of the revolutionary terrorists either joined the movement or suspended their own activities in order to
give the Gandhian mass movement a chance.


But the sudden suspension of the Non-Cooperation Movement shattered the high hopes raised earlier. Many young people began to
question the very basic strategy of the national leadership and its emphasis on nonviolence and began to look for alternatives. They were
not attracted by the parliamentary politics of the Swarajists or the patient and undramatic constructive work of the no-changers. Many
were drawn to the idea that violent methods alone would free India. Revolutionary terrorism again became attractive. It is not accidental
that nearly all the major new leaders of the revolutionary terrorist politics, for example, Jogesh Chandra Chatterjea, Surya Sen, Jatin Das,
Chandrashekhar Azad, Bhagat Singh, Sukhdev, Shiv Varma, Bhagwati Charan Vohra and Jaidev Kapur, had been enthusiastic participants
in the non-violent Non-Cooperation Movement. Gradually two separate strands of revolutionary terrorism developed - one in Punjab, U.P.
and Bihar and the other in Bengal. Both the strands came under the influence of several new social forces. One was the upsurge of
working-class trade unionism after the War. They could see the revolutionary potential of the new class and desired to harness it to the
nationalist revolution. The second major influence was that of the Russian Revolution and the success of the young Socialist State in
consolidating itself. The youthful revolutionaries were keen to learn from and take the help of the young Soviet State and its ruling
Bolshevik Party. The third influence was that of the newly sprouting Communist groups with their emphasis on Marxism, Socialism and
the proletariat. (Extracted with edits from www.chronicleindia.in)

Peasants were worried about the future not just because they had more cause for worry, but also because they could do something about
it. They could clear another field, dig another irrigation canal, sow more crops.


The anxious peasant was as frenetic and hardworking as a harvester ant in the summer, sweating to plant olive trees whose oil would be
pressed by his children and grandchildren, putting off until the winter or the following year the eating of the food he craved today. The
stress of farming had far-reaching consequences. It was the foundation of large-scale political and social systems. Sadly, the diligent
peasants almost never achieved the future economic security they so craved through their hard work in the present. Everywhere, rulers
and elites sprang up, living off the peasants' surplus food and leaving them with only a bare subsistence. These forfeited food surpluses
fuelled politics, wars, art and philosophy. They built palaces, forts, monuments and temples. Until the late modern era, more than 90 per
cent of humans were peasants who rose each morning to till the land by the sweat of their brows. The extra they produced fed the tiny
minority of elites - kings, government officials, soldiers, priests, artists and thinkers - who fill the history books. History is something that
very few people have been doing while everyone else was ploughing fields and carrying water buckets.

In the summer of 1989, the American magazine The National Interest published an essay titled "The End of History?". Its author, political
scientist Francis Fukuyama, argued that the great ideological battles between East and West were over and that Western liberal
democracy had triumphed. With anti-communist protests sweeping across the Soviet bloc, the claim appeared timely. When his book The
End of History and the Last Man appeared three years later, the question mark had been removed.


Fukuyama clarified that he was not suggesting that events would cease or that all nations would become liberal democracies. Rather, he
argued that societies would no longer claim to represent fundamentally different or superior ideological systems. His focus was on ideas,
not events. He maintained that Western liberal democracy, balancing liberty and equality, represented the endpoint of mankind's
ideological evolution and would, in the long run, remain the only broadly credible form of government.


Drawing on Hegel's philosophy, Fukuyama described history as a linear progression shaped by technological development and the
resolution of conflict. Humanity, in this view, moves through stages-from tribal to feudal to industrial society. While Marx saw communism
as the culmination of this process, Fukuyama proposed liberal democracy as the final stage.


He also suggested that this "end of history" would bring a different kind of world, where ideological struggle would give way to economic
calculation, technical problem-solving, and the satisfaction of consumer demands.


The transformation marked not the end of events, but the conclusion of ideological evolution as a driving force in human history.


(Extracted with edits from The Guardian)

In discussions about China's political philosophy, the idea of unity often appears as a central theme. This notion is not merely
administrative but deeply rooted in historical and cultural narratives. For centuries, Chinese thinkers have argued that internal unity
ensures stability, while disorder invites suffering. This belief is often linked to the concept of tianxia, or "all under heaven," which imagines
the world as a single, harmonious system under moral authority.


However, the interpretation of this idea has not remained constant. In ancient times, unity was associated with ethical governance: rulers
were expected to maintain harmony through virtue rather than force. Yet in modern contexts, critics argue that the same idea is used more
strategically. They suggest that appeals to unity can sometimes justify strict control, presenting dissent not as a legitimate difference of
opinion but as a threat to collective well-being.

Supporters of the unity principle counter that such criticism misunderstands its purpose. According to them, unity is not about
suppressing diversity but about preventing fragmentation that could weaken the state. They point to periods in Chinese history where
political division led to conflict and instability, arguing that a strong, unified system is necessary for long-term prosperity.


Still, some scholars remain skeptical. They note that historical narratives are often selectively interpreted to support present goals. For
instance, episodes of unity are highlighted as ideal, while periods of diversity or decentralisation are portrayed negatively. This selective
reading, critics argue, creates a simplified version of history that may overlook the complexity of past societies.


Thus, the debate over unity is not simply about political structure, but about how history itself is understood and used. Whether unity
represents a genuine cultural value or a convenient political tool remains a matter of ongoing discussion, with each perspective offering its
own interpretation of both past and present.

In Moulmein, in lower Burma, I was hated by large numbers of people - the only time in my life that I have been important enough for this
to happen to me. I was sub-divisional police officer of the town, and in an aimless, petty kind of way anti-European feeling was very bitter.
No one had the guts to raise a riot, but if a European woman went through the bazaars alone somebody would probably spit betel juice
over her dress. As a police officer I was an obvious target and was baited whenever it seemed safe to do so. When a nimble Burman
tripped me up on the football field and the referee (another Burman) looked the other way, the crowd yelled with hideous laughter.


This happened more than once. In the end the sneering yellow faces of young men that met me everywhere, the insults hooted after me
when I was at a safe distance, got badly on my nerves. The young Buddhist priests were the worst of all. There were several thousands of
them in the town and none of them seemed to have anything to do except stand on street corners and jeer at Europeans. All this was
perplexing and upsetting. For at that time I had already made up my mind that imperialism was an evil thing and the sooner I chucked up
my job and got out of it the better. Theoretically - and secretly, of course - I was all for the Burmese and all against their oppressors, the
British. As for the job I was doing, I hated it more bitterly than I can perhaps make clear. In a job like that you see the dirty work of Empire
at close quarters. The wretched prisoners huddling in the stinking cages of the lock-ups, the grey, cowed faces of the long-term convicts,
the scarred buttocks of the men who had been Bogged with bamboos - all these oppressed me with an intolerable sense of guilt. But I
could get nothing into perspective. I was young and ill-educated and I had had to think out my problems in the utter silence that is imposed
on every Englishman in the East. I did not even know that the British Empire is dying, still less did I know that it is a great deal better than
the younger empires that are going to supplant it. All I knew was that I was stuck between my hatred of the empire I served and my rage
against the evil-spirited little beasts who tried to make my job impossible.


(Extracted with edits from Shooting an Elephant by George Orwell)

Sriharikota on April 10, 2026. In this test, a simulated Crew Module, weighing about 5.7 tonnes that is equivalent to the mass of the Crew

Under the law of torts, nuisance refers to an unlawful interference with a person's use or enjoyment of land, or of some right over or in
connection with it. Nuisance may be classified as public or private. A public nuisance affects the rights of the public at large, such as
obstruction of a public way, whereas a private nuisance involves substantial and unreasonable interference with an individual's enjoyment
of land.


The determination of nuisance depends on multiple factors, including the locality, duration, intensity, and the nature of the interference.
What may be considered nuisance in a quiet residential area may not be so in an industrial locality. The law does not protect against trivial
or fanciful inconveniences; the interference must be real and substantial.


Further, even lawful acts may constitute nuisance if they cause unreasonable interference. Conversely, the existence of malice may
aggravate liability but is not essential to establish nuisance. In certain situations, defences such as statutory authority or prescription may
be available, though mere utility of the defendant's conduct is not a complete defence.


A prescriptive right may be acquired where the defendant has openly and continuously carried on the activity causing nuisance for a
period of twenty years without interruption, as of right. However, the right is limited to the extent and manner in which the activity was
previously enjoyed, and any substantial increase in the interference may still amount to nuisance.


In cases of public nuisance, an individual may bring an action only if they suffer special damage beyond that suffered by the general
public. Remedies for nuisance include damages, injunction, or abatement, depending on the circumstances.

The rule against double jeopardy is a fundamental protection in criminal law, embodied in Article 20(2) of the Constitution of India, which
provides that no person shall be prosecuted and punished for the same offence more than once. The protection applies only when there
has been both prosecution and punishment in a prior proceeding.


This principle is distinct from the broader common law doctrines reflected in Section 300 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, which
bars a second trial for the same offence or for any other offence based on the same facts for which the accused could have been charged
in the first trial. However, the bar applies only when the earlier proceeding was before a court of competent jurisdiction and resulted in a
conviction or acquittal. The protection does not apply to departmental or administrative proceedings, as these are not considered
"prosecution" in the strict sense. Similarly, if the ingredients of the two offences are distinct, even if arising from the same facts,
subsequent prosecution may be permissible. Further, the doctrine applies only when the offences are identical in law and fact; mere
similarity in allegations or factual overlap is insufficient. The focus is on whether the second proceeding seeks to punish the accused
again for the same offence.

Criminal law distinguishes between offences involving unlawful taking of property based not merely on the act of taking, but on the
manner in which the taking occurs, the state of mind of the offender, and the circumstances surrounding the act.


At its most basic level, theft involves the dishonest taking of movable property out of the possession of another without consent. Consent
here refers to free and voluntary agreement; therefore, where property is taken stealthily, secretly, or without the knowledge of the person
in possession, the absence of consent is clear. Importantly, theft does not require the use of force, threat, or confrontation. The offence is
complete the moment property is moved with dishonest intention.


However, the law treats certain forms of taking more seriously. Where the act of theft is accompanied by violence, threat, or fear of
immediate harm, the offence is elevated to robbery. The distinguishing feature is not merely that force is used, but that such force or
threat is closely connected in time with the act of taking or carrying away the property. Even the fear of instant harm, if it compels a person
to part with possession, may convert what appears to be voluntary delivery into a coerced act. Thus, consent obtained under immediate
fear is not true consent in the eyes of law.

The law further recognises that crimes committed by groups pose greater danger to society. When five or more persons act together in
committing or attempting such violent taking, or even if some of them merely assist or stand ready to assist, the offence is classified as
dacoity. What matters is collective participation, not whether each individual physically commits the act of taking. Even passive roles such
as keeping watch, blocking escape routes, or facilitating the offence may be sufficient to attract liability.


It is also important to distinguish between preparation and attempt. Mere gathering of individuals with intent, without any step towards
execution, may not amount to the offence itself, though it may be punishable separately. Similarly, the presence of force alone does not
automatically elevate theft to robbery unless it is used in order to commit the taking or to retain the stolen property.


Thus, classification depends on a careful analysis of:
• whether there was consent or merely submission under fear
• whether force or threat was used, and at what stage
• whether the act was individual or collective
• and whether the conduct amounts to preparation, attempt, or completion
